summary: Discusses how a new network device in a remote location could be installed and configured without sending staff to the site, even where "remote hands" support exists. It extends existing vendor proprietary auto-install mechanisms to give the initial configuration limited confidentiality during bootstrapping. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Setting up a new gadget in a faraway room normally means someone has to travel there. This document describes a way to send the gadget its starting settings from afar while keeping them private.

questions: how to securely install a network device remotely
how do network devices get their configuration
subtitle: Protecting network device configurations during remote installation

tldr.problem: Network device configurations contain security secrets and proprietary information. Operators must physically travel to remote locations to avoid exposing these secrets when installing and configuring new devices.
tldr.mechanism: When a device generates its public-private key pair during manufacturing, the operator can encrypt the initial configuration to that device's public key. The device then decrypts it using its private key after fetching it from the network, protecting confidentiality in transit and at rest.
tldr.outcome: This allows secure remote device installation without requiring an operator to travel on-site or risking exposure of sensitive configuration data to untrusted parties.

today: RFC 8886 is an Informational RFC and remains the standard way for vendors to enable secure bootstrapping of network devices with encrypted initial configurations.

sections.title: The Problem with Remote Device Setup
sections.content:
Network device configurations hold sensitive information: secrets for RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication, proprietary settings, and security-related data. Many network devices use auto-install: they get an IP address via DHCP, fetch configuration from a server (often via TFTP), and boot up. But sending unencrypted configurations to remote sites, or asking remote staff to install them, exposes these secrets to eavesdropping or theft.

This document extends existing vendor proprietary auto-install mechanisms with encryption to protect the confidentiality of initial configuration during bootstrapping.
sections.plainLanguage: Network gadgets usually download their settings in plain view. This is risky for secret stuff. This document shows how to scramble them.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
Most network devices already include auto-install logic. They use DHCP or DHCPv6 to get an IP address and the address of a configuration server, then download their configuration by serial number or media access control (MAC) address. This document extends that by allowing the configuration file to be encrypted.

The process uses the device's serial number (or another unique identifier) as a device identifier. The device publishes its public key during manufacturing; the operator fetches the device's certificate by providing the serial number, encrypts the configuration using that public key, and places it on their local configuration server. When the device boots, it uses DHCP to find the configuration server, downloads the encrypted file, and decrypts it with its private key.
sections.plainLanguage: The gadget gets a secret key when built. Its maker publishes the public part. The operator scrambles the settings with that public key, and the gadget unscrambles them with its secret key.

sections.title: What the Vendor Does
sections.content:
During manufacturing, when a device first powers on, it generates a public-private key pair and publishes the public key (usually as an X.509 certificate) to the vendor's directory server. The directory server accepts certificates only from the manufacturing facility and checks they match vendor-defined policies. Some constrained devices may send only the raw public key and unique identifier; more capable devices generate and send self-signed certificates.

X.509 certificates are used as a convenient serialization format because of widespread tooling support on network devices, though most of the certificate metadata for revocation and aging is ignored by the consumer, which instead pins the end-entity key fingerprint.
sections.plainLanguage: The gadget makes a secret pair when it's born at the factory. It tells the maker's server about the public part. The maker keeps this on file for the operator to download later.

sections.title: What the Operator Does
sections.content:
When a new device arrives, the operator contacts the vendor's server with the device's serial number and downloads the certificate. The operator fetches it using secure transport (such as HTTPS) to authenticate the source. The operator then encrypts the initial configuration (for example, using S/MIME) with the public key in the certificate and places the encrypted configuration on their local configuration server (such as TFTP).

When the device boots and discovers it is unconfigured, it uses existing auto-install functionality: it performs DHCP Discovery to get an IP address and configuration server, contacts the server, and downloads its configuration file. The device determines whether the configuration is encrypted (for example, via magic string, file extension, or DHCP option), and if encrypted, it decrypts it with its private key and installs it.
sections.plainLanguage: The operator gets the public part from the maker's server using the serial number. The operator scrambles the settings with it and puts the locked version on their server. The gadget downloads it, uses its secret key to unscramble it, and starts up.

sections.title: What It Protects and What It Does Not
sections.content:
This design provides object-level security: confidentiality for the configuration stored at rest on the configuration server and while in transit between the configuration server and the device, even if the underlying transport does not provide this security.

It does not protect the source of the encrypted configuration or prevent theft and reuse of devices. An attacker with physical access to the device before it connects to the network, or who exploits it after installation, may be able to extract the private key (especially if not stored in a trusted platform module) and download encrypted configuration files. An attacker with access to the configuration server and the device's public key could return a malicious configuration. The mechanism does not protect against a malicious vendor who generates the key pair off the device and keeps a copy of the private key.

Even so, security-conscious operators may wish to bootstrap devices with a minimal configuration and then replace it with a complete one after the device is installed in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: The scrambling protects the settings from snooping. But if someone steals the gadget or hacks the server, they might get in. It is not a complete solution, but it makes things much safer than sending settings in plain view.
